chapter_title: Rotational Motion and Rigid Body Dynamics
learning_objectives: Calculate moment of inertia for discrete point masses and continuous bodies using integration and the parallel/perpendicular axis theorems.
Formulate rotational equations of motion tau = I alpha and apply work-energy principles to fixed axis rotation.
Determine the angular momentum of particles and rigid bodies about fixed reference points and instantaneous axes of rotation.
Apply the principle of conservation of angular momentum to isolated systems with time-varying moments of inertia.
Analyze pure rolling kinematics and dynamics on horizontal and inclined surfaces under static friction constraints.
Determine critical conditions for sliding versus toppling of rigid bodies on rough planes.

formula_sequence.title: Moment of Inertia of Discrete Point Masses

variables.I: Moment of inertia about the specified axis
variables.r_i: Perpendicular distance of the i-th particle from the axis

assumptions: Point mass particles with negligible individual extents
Strictly perpendicular radial distances measured from the rotation axis
Rigid spatial configuration among all particles
validity_conditions: Universal definition for any finite system of discrete particles in classical mechanics
common_misuse: Using direct vector distance from an origin instead of perpendicular distance from the axis
Assuming moment of inertia is an intrinsic scalar independent of axis location

formula_sequence.title: Moments of Inertia for Standard Symmetrical Continuous Rigid Bodies
formula_sequence.equation: I_{\text{ring}} = M R^2, \quad I_{\text{disc}} = \frac{1}{2} M R^2, \quad I_{\text{rod}} = \frac{1}{12} M L^2, \quad I_{\text{solid sphere}} = \frac{2}{5} M R^2, \quad I_{\text{hollow sphere}} = \frac{2}{3} M R^2

variables.M: Total mass of the rigid body
variables.R: Radius of circular cross-section or sphere

assumptions: Uniform homogeneous mass distribution with constant density
Axes pass through centroid along principal symmetry directions
Thin rod and thin spherical shell approximations where wall thicknesses are negligible
validity_conditions: Applies strictly to symmetric uniform bodies about their designated centroidal axes
common_misuse: Confusing rod moment of inertia about center (1/12 M L^2) with moment of inertia about end (1/3 M L^2)
Using 2/5 M R^2 for hollow spheres or 2/3 M R^2 for solid spheres

formula_sequence.title: Parallel Axis Theorem

variables.I: Moment of inertia about parallel axis
variables.I_{\\text{cm}}: Moment of inertia about parallel axis through center of mass
variables.d: Perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes

assumptions: Rigid body assumption
Both axes are strictly parallel
One axis passes strictly through the center of mass
validity_conditions: Applicable to three-dimensional rigid bodies of arbitrary geometry for any pair of parallel axes where one is a centroidal axis
common_misuse: Applying theorem between two arbitrary parallel axes neither of which passes through the center of mass
Using linear distance instead of perpendicular distance

formula_sequence.title: Perpendicular Axis Theorem for Planar Laminas

variables.I_z: Moment of inertia about normal axis perpendicular to lamina through origin O
variables.I_x: Moment of inertia about coplanar x-axis passing through O
variables.I_y: Moment of inertia about coplanar y-axis passing through O

assumptions: Rigid body is strictly a two-dimensional planar lamina lying entirely in the xy-plane (z = 0)
All three axes x, y, and z are mutually perpendicular and intersect at a single concurrent origin O
validity_conditions: Strictly valid ONLY for two-dimensional planar laminar bodies; fails identically for three-dimensional bodies
common_misuse: Applying the theorem to three-dimensional objects (e.g. solid cylinders or spheres)
Using axes that do not intersect at a common coplanar point

formula_sequence.title: Radius of Gyration

variables.k: Radius of gyration about the specified axis
variables.I: Moment of inertia about the specified axis
variables.M: Total mass of the rigid body

assumptions: Rigid body of total mass M
Specified fixed axis of rotation
validity_conditions: Universal geometric definition representing the effective distance at which whole mass could be concentrated
common_misuse: Treating radius of gyration as an intrinsic geometric constant independent of axis location

formula_sequence.title: Definition and Moment Arm Representation of Torque

variables.\\tau: Torque vector about reference point O
variables.r: Position vector from reference point O to point of application of force
variables.\\theta: Angle between position vector r and force vector F
variables.r_\\perp: Moment arm (perpendicular distance from O to line of action of force)

assumptions: Specified fixed reference origin O in an inertial reference frame
Line of action of force is well-defined
validity_conditions: Universal definition of moment of a force in classical mechanics
common_misuse: Omitting reference point specification; torque has no physical meaning without specifying reference point
Using vector length |r| instead of perpendicular moment arm r_perp = r sin(theta)

formula_sequence.title: Angular Kinematic Equations Under Constant Angular Acceleration
assumptions: Fixed rotation axis with invariant spatial orientation
Constant angular acceleration alpha over the entire time interval
validity_conditions: Strictly invalid if angular acceleration alpha varies with time or angle
common_misuse: Applying these equations to variable torque / variable alpha systems
Using angles in degrees or revolutions without converting to radians

formula_sequence.title: Torque Dynamic Relation

variables.I: Moment of inertia about rotation axis

assumptions: Rigid body
Fixed rotation axis or rotation about center of mass
Axis is principal axis of inertia
validity_conditions: Holds in inertial frame or in accelerating frame if pseudo-force torques about CM are accounted for
common_misuse: Using \tau = I \alpha about an arbitrary accelerating point without pseudo-force torque
Ignoring non-principal axis cross-products

formula_sequence.title: Rotational Kinetic Energy of a Rigid Body

variables.I: Moment of inertia about the axis of rotation
variables.\\omega: Angular velocity of the rigid body

assumptions: Rigid body rotating about a fixed axis or about a principal axis passing through center of mass
Uniform angular velocity omega for all constituent mass elements
validity_conditions: Universal relation for rigid body rotation in classical mechanics
common_misuse: Using moment of inertia about center of mass when body rotates about a different off-center fixed pivot
Adding 1/2 M v_cm^2 when calculating pure rotation about a fixed pivot

formula_sequence.title: Rotational Work-Energy Theorem

variables.W_{\\text{net}}: Net work done by external torques
variables.\\tau_{\\text{net}}: Net external torque about the rotation axis
variables.I: Moment of inertia about the fixed rotation axis

assumptions: Rigid body rotating about a fixed axis in an inertial reference frame
Work evaluated between initial angle theta_1 and final angle theta_2
validity_conditions: Valid for any net torque function whether constant or angle-dependent
common_misuse: Multiplying torque by time instead of angular displacement to compute work
Confusing rotational work with angular impulse (tau * dt)

formula_sequence.title: Particle Angular Momentum

variables.r: Position vector from origin O to particle

assumptions: Point mass particle
Reference point O is explicitly specified in an inertial frame
validity_conditions: Universal definition for point mass particle in classical mechanics
common_misuse: Assuming a particle moving in a straight line has zero angular momentum
Omitting origin dependency

formula_sequence.title: Angular Momentum of Rigid Body in Planar Motion About Arbitrary Origin

variables.\\vec{L}_O: Total angular momentum vector about reference origin O
variables.I_{\\text{cm}}: Moment of inertia about principal axis through center of mass
variables.\\vec{\\omega}: Angular velocity vector of the rigid body
variables.\\vec{r}_{\\text{cm}}: Position vector of center of mass relative to origin O
variables.M: Total mass of the rigid body
variables.\\vec{v}_{\\text{cm}}: Linear velocity vector of center of mass

assumptions: Planar motion where angular velocity vector is perpendicular to the translational plane
Rigid body condition with constant mass M
Origin O is an unaccelerated fixed reference point in an inertial frame
validity_conditions: Universal decomposition of angular momentum into spin and orbital components for general plane motion
common_misuse: Omitting orbital term r_cm x M v_cm when calculating angular momentum about an external pivot
Using moment of inertia about an arbitrary point instead of center of mass in the spin term

formula_sequence.title: Conservation of Angular Momentum About Fixed Axis

variables.I_i: Initial moment of inertia about axis
variables.I_f: Final moment of inertia about axis

assumptions: Net external torque about the designated rotation axis vanishes (\tau_{\text{ext}, z} = 0)
validity_conditions: Valid for isolated systems or systems with zero net torque along a specific axis
common_misuse: Assuming kinetic energy is also conserved when internal reconfiguration occurs
Applying conservation along an axis experiencing external torque

formula_sequence.title: Pure Rolling Kinematic Constraint and Velocity Distribution

variables.v_{\\text{cm}}: Linear speed of center of mass
variables.v_P: Instantaneous velocity of contact point P on stationary ground
variables.v_{\\text{top}}: Instantaneous velocity of top rim point

assumptions: Rigid wheel or cylinder rolling on a stationary flat horizontal surface
Zero relative sliding at the instantaneous contact point (pure rolling)
validity_conditions: Holds strictly during pure rolling; if the surface itself moves with speed v_s, constraint becomes v_cm - v_s = R omega
common_misuse: Assuming top point has speed v_cm instead of 2 v_cm
Assuming contact point has zero acceleration because its instantaneous velocity is zero

formula_sequence.title: Acceleration and Critical Friction for Pure Rolling on an Inclined Plane

variables.a_{\\text{cm}}: Linear acceleration of center of mass down the incline
variables.\\theta: Inclination angle of plane with horizontal
variables.I_{\\text{cm}}: Moment of inertia about center of mass
variables.\\mu_{\\min}: Minimum coefficient of static friction to prevent slipping

assumptions: Uniform symmetrical rigid body rolling down an incline of angle theta
Sufficient static friction mu_s >= mu_min to ensure zero slipping
Rigid circular contact profile
validity_conditions: Valid strictly for pure rolling without slipping; if mu_s < mu_min, body slips with a = g(sin theta - mu_k cos theta)
common_misuse: Using translational acceleration g sin(theta) for a rolling body
Assuming rolling acceleration depends on the body's mass or radius rather than purely on the dimensionless ratio k^2/R^2

formula_sequence.title: Critical Threshold Conditions for Toppling versus Sliding

variables.F_{\\text{crit}}: Critical horizontal force causing toppling on flat ground
variables.b: Base width of block along direction of force
variables.H: Height above ground at which lateral force is applied
variables.\\theta_{\\text{crit}}: Critical incline tilt angle causing toppling before sliding

assumptions: Uniform homogeneous rectangular/cuboidal block resting on rough ground
Normal reaction force shifts to extreme tipping edge at toppling threshold
Coulomb friction model with static coefficient mu_s
validity_conditions: Toppling precedes sliding on horizontal ground if b / (2 H) < mu_s; toppling precedes sliding on incline if b / h < mu_s
common_misuse: Assuming toppling occurs about center of mass rather than the tipping base edge
Ignoring friction coefficient when determining whether body slides first or tips first

misconception_sequence.statement: Straight-line motion cannot have angular momentum
misconception_sequence.explanation: Angular momentum L = r x p depends on the reference point, not circular curvature.
misconception_sequence.trap_mechanism: Particle moving along y = d evaluated at origin.

misconception_sequence.statement: Conservation of angular momentum implies conservation of kinetic energy
misconception_sequence.explanation: Radial mass repositioning requires internal work that alters rotational kinetic energy.

misconception_sequence.statement: Applying perpendicular axis theorem to three-dimensional bodies
misconception_sequence.explanation: Holds strictly for 2D laminas where z = 0 identically.
misconception_sequence.trap_mechanism: Applying I_z = I_x + I_y to solid cylinder or sphere.

misconception_sequence.statement: Assuming equal string tension across a massive accelerating pulley
misconception_sequence.explanation: Accelerating pulley requires net torque (T_1 - T_2) R = I alpha.

misconception_sequence.statement: Believing static friction in pure rolling always opposes linear velocity
misconception_sequence.explanation: Static friction opposes slip at contact point and can act forward.
misconception_sequence.trap_mechanism: Spool pulled by horizontal string above center of percussion.

misconception_sequence.statement: Believing contact point in pure rolling has zero acceleration
misconception_sequence.explanation: Instantaneous velocity is zero, but centripetal acceleration is omega^2 R upward.

revision_checklist: Distinguish perpendicular distance r_perp from coordinate distance in moment of inertia integrals.
Check that perpendicular axis theorem is applied strictly to 2D planar laminas.
Remember that string tensions differ across a massive pulley.
Verify reference point O when evaluating torque and angular momentum.
In pure rolling, verify v_cm = R omega and a_cm = R alpha at contact with stationary surface.
Recall that static friction can act forward, backward, or be zero depending on point of force application.
Use rolling acceleration down incline a_cm = g sin(theta) / (1 + k^2/R^2).
Check toppling condition F h = M g (b/2) and compare with sliding threshold mu_s M g.
